definition: Sylvan means relating to woods and forests.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word sylvan. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know sylvan should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The trail turns sylvan past the second bridge, where the sky narrows to a ribbon between two walls of oak.
Shaded says only that something blocks the sun — a porch awning will do it; it is the faintest claim on this scale, far short of sylvan, where the woods own the scene entirely.
Leafy goes further than shaded — green branches genuinely around you, a street of old maples; sylvan claims the most: the woods own the scene entirely, deep and storied enough for a midsummer play.

Wooded is the plain word for tree-covered ground: trees grow here, and that is the entire claim — no mood, no story. Sylvan reports the same trees and adds the spell, the green world of folk tales and deep summer.

Forested is the forester's and the report's word — a tally of hectares under trees, measurable and mood-free. Sylvan gives the same land its glamour: it says the woods are there and that they enchant, both in one word.

The set designer's brief for the forest act was a single word: sylvan.

Her sketches show what she took it to mean — birches rising clean out of sight into the flies, moss padding every step, lanterns rigged to drop the light in green pools, a floor built to swallow every footfall.
The audience, she told the carpenters, should feel the town left far behind them.
Sylvan is the exact word for that stage, because it means relating to woods and forests — and it brings a glow the plainer words lack.
A lot can be tree-covered; a scene is sylvan when the forest itself is the enchantment, the green world of folk tales and midsummer plays.
It tells you about the trees and about the spell at the same time.
Sylvan is a stage-lit word: reach for it when the forest is the romance — poems, playbills, travel writing at its dreamiest.
On a survey or a zoning map, wooded and forested do the honest work.
Keep it apart from this unit's verdant, which is about green growth anywhere — a golf course can be verdant with not a tree on it, and a pine wood in snow is sylvan with no green at all.

The Ramble in Central Park looks like a piece of wild woodland that Manhattan somehow forgot to pave.
In fact every boulder, stream, and crooked path was placed there by the park's designers in the 1860s.
Frederick Law Olmsted wanted city dwellers to step out of the grid into a sylvan scene — winding green shadows, birdsong, water heard before it is seen.
He argued that such scenery worked on tired minds the way rest works on tired muscles.
The illusion holds: stand in the middle of the Ramble today and the towers vanish behind a wall of summer leaves.
